title: A Preposterous, Overpriced, Beautiful Disaster of a Car
excerpt: The most important Cybertruck ever built is probably still parked somewhere on the grounds of Mar-a-Lago
body: The most important Cybertruck ever built is probably still parked somewhere on the grounds of Mar-a-Lago
In August 2024, Donald Trump stood on the driveway of his Palm Beach club and circled a custom version of Tesla’s notorious, angular electric truck

Wrapped in a giant photo of his bloodied face after the assassination attempt that summer, the car was a gift from the MAGA influencer Adin Ross during a livestreamed interview. “Wow, that’s an Elon!” Trump said
When Trump returned to the presidency, Elon Musk’s truck became a defining symbol of his second term—a MAGA hat on wheels
Like the president himself, the Cybertruck is thought of differently by different people: brash, unsophisticated, or badass
And like the world’s richest man and former head of DOGE, the Cybertruck moves fast and breaks things with little regard for anything in its way

If nothing else, the Cybertruck is unique: Here is a car that is marketed as bulletproof and has a windshield wiper (only one wiper) that Musk has compared to a “katana.” Now the Cybertruck is about to be something else: discontinued

Early this morning, Musk announced on X that he will wind down production of the Cybertruck by the middle of next year to free up factory space to make Cybercabs, the robotaxis that Tesla is attempting to roll out across the country
No matter how you feel about it, the Cybertruck will go down as a tremendous flop in Silicon Valley history
When the car was first released, in November 2023, Musk called it the “best product” that he’s ever released
As Musk bankrolled Trump’s 2024 presidential run and then joined him in Washington, MAGA supporters enthusiastically embraced the Cybertruck
Fast-forward to 2026, and almost no one wants to buy one
The shift has been telling: The midterms were disastrous for Musk, who blew nearly $500 million boosting unsuccessful Republican candidates, especially in Texas, where Tesla is based

Musk’s discontinuation of the Cybertruck may be seen, among other things, as political triage, a way of wiping his hands clean of a car that liberals have branded as the “Deplorean.” [ Read: My day inside America’s most hated car ] Still, it would be a mistake to remember the truck as nothing more than the apotheosis of two years of Trumpian (and Muskian) excess
The Cybertruck was a meme and a culture-war totem, but it was also just a car
And on that front, Musk’s creation was especially a letdown

When he first announced the car in 2019, it was a revelation, no matter how ugly: After proving that electric cars could be more than just souped-up golf carts, his car company would now bring EVs to the masses
The Cybertruck, Musk promised, would start at just $40,000, a fraction of the cost of Tesla’s other cars at the time
By the time the Cybertruck was actually for sale, it came with a sticker price of $100,000
In some ways, the truck was doomed from the beginning: Building a vehicle that ignores the principles of basic aerodynamics isn’t exactly cheap or easy

Dogged by one problem after the next—stainless-steel panels that can fall off, a faulty accelerator pedal that can get stuck and turn the car into a cruise missile—the Cybertruck did not entice very many people to actually put up the money for one
Within a week of the vehicle’s unveiling, Musk said that 250,000 had preordered one
But in three years, he has sold a total of only 70,000 Cybertrucks
In spite of all the problems, the Cybertruck actually is a pretty fun car
It’s difficult to maneuver and more than a little impractical
But you can’t take a Zoom call from the front seat of a Toyota Camry, or have that vehicle make fart noises when a passenger sits down
Musk’s creation was absurd, but it was different
America desperately needs what the Cybertruck could have been
Electric cars offer the possibility of redesigning vehicles from the ground up
In China, you can buy EVs with built-in fridges and headlights that can project movies
In the U.S., however, automakers have mostly just duped the gas cars we’re all familiar with
Even during this moment of high gas prices, Americans have been stubbornly unwilling to go electric
It’s hard not to wonder how many more electric cars would be on the streets if the Cybertruck had actually lived up to its original promise
The Cybertruck was not the best product Musk ever made—not even close—but it’s the product that reveals the most about his motivations and impulses

It is a cautionary tale of Musk’s habit of overpromising and under-delivering. (Data centers in space! Robots that can water your plants !) Most of all, the Cybertruck is another reminder—in this case, a nearly 7,000-pound one—that the influence of the world’s richest man does have limits.

title: Harmeet Dhillon’s Tenure of Destruction
excerpt: Harmeet Dhillon is not the most notable administration official to depart after Democrats’ enormous midterm victory—that title goes to White House Chief of Staf
body: Harmeet Dhillon is not the most notable administration official to depart after Democrats’ enormous midterm victory—that title goes to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, who President Trump announced today would be replaced by Stephen Miller
But Dhillon’s short tenure shows the immense influence that Trump has had on the federal government in less than two years in power
Her departure comes as Democrats prepare a long list of investigations they hope to pursue once they take control of the House and Senate in January

As results streamed in on Tuesday night, Robert Garcia, the incoming head of the House Oversight Committee, issued a two-word statement to Trump appointees: “Lawyer up.” Jamie Raskin, the presumptive head of the Judiciary Committee, has promised intense scrutiny of the Justice Department
Having stepped down, Dhillon will have more time to spend with her lawyers ahead of the inevitable hearings
Dhillon had reportedly been campaigning for a promotion to a higher position at DOJ, which was apparently not forthcoming
CBS News reports that Trump wanted her fired for remarks about the supposed crisis of voting by noncitizens in a recent 60 Minutes interview that he found insufficiently bellicose

But she can depart with the satisfaction of completing the task she set out to achieve: doing immense damage to the Civil Rights Division, long known as the “crown jewel” of the department. “We changed it, and that’s what we came here to do,” she told Fox News . “And it’s done.” She’s right

Dhillon’s goal, my colleague Quinta Jurecic wrote in a definitive April profile , was to reshape the division in Trump’s name and turn its historic focus on protecting civil rights upside down. “She has used the branch’s resources to investigate school districts and colleges over DEI, back the White House’s push to gain Republican congressional seats through redistricting, and prosecute journalists covering an anti-ICE protest in Minnesota,” Quina wrote

The division also gave up on holding police departments accountable for civil-rights abuses, abandoning proposed agreements with departments in Minneapolis and Louisville, Kentucky, that resulted from investigations after the murders of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor
But as the midterms drew closer, a major focus was elections
Under Dhillon, the division pursued debunked and baseless claims of election fraud in Fulton County, Georgia, during the 2020 election
After the Supreme Court effectively threw out Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act this spring, Dhillon leaped to push states to redraw maps in order to reduce minority voting power
She twisted states’ arms to hand over voter rolls, part of a futile attempt by the administration to find evidence of widespread voting by noncitizens
This pressure continued right up to Election Day

In the closing weeks of the campaign, the Justice Department tried to intimidate local and state election officials in states including California, Washington, and Alaska—aiming to put a thumb on the scales in service of Republican candidates
As the Cato Institute’s Walter Olson writes , the Trump administration failed to subvert the election, but not because it didn’t try
When a president of a different party takes over the Justice Department, priorities naturally change
But some changes go beyond those normal shifts of emphasis
Bush administration, an inspector general’s report described sweeping and improper politicization
In that instance, some 70 percent of attorneys left the division between 2003 and 2007
By comparison, as much as 80 percent of the division’s staff have left in the less than two years of the Trump presidency
Dhillon’s Civil Right Division did have some notable failures
For example, the attempt to acquire voter rolls was a flop
The administration suffered an astonishing string of 27 losses in federal district courts in related cases, and drew harsh criticism even from Republican state officials

As one last indignity, lawyers from the Civil Rights Division failed to obtain an indictment from a grand jury for Cassidy Hutchinson, a former Trump aide who testified to the House January 6 Committee
Outside observers noted that bringing civil-rights charges against Hutchinson, rather than simply charging her with false statements, was a peculiar choice
In sum, Dhillon leaves the Civil Rights Division in terrible shape: Its ranks are depleted, its work is interrupted, and its credibility with juries and judges is in tatters

Justice Connection, an advocacy group for former DOJ employees, issued a statement decrying her tenure. “After she upended the division’s mission-critical work, the civil servants who dedicated their careers to protecting vulnerable communities were instead told to target them—and more than three-quarters of the division’s lawyers left,” Stacey Young, its executive director, said. “For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded
Dhillon decimated it.” Dhillon might have been able to boil the same sentiment down to just two words: Mission accomplished .

title: A Monster of His Time
excerpt: The criminal trial of Russell Brand took less than four weeks, at the end of which the comedian turned spiritual influencer was found guilty of one count of rap
body: The criminal trial of Russell Brand took less than four weeks, at the end of which the comedian turned spiritual influencer was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. (The jury in London declared him not guilty of three other charges, two of rape and one of attempted indecent assault.) The accounts detailed by Brand’s accusers were harrowing

The Christianity-themed podcast episodes broadcast by Brand and his wife, Laura, before and during the trial—their regular series is titled Sunday Service With the Brands —were so audacious that they were hard to process

In one installment , Brand interrupted his own monologue on how a Bible passage from Ephesians helped him prepare for court each day (“Stand firm then, with the belt of truth buckled round your waist”) so that he could read a sponsored ad for Polymarket
Still, what shocked me most during the trial was how many of the women detailed assaults that they said happened to them while they were at work

One complainant testified that while she was employed at MTV in 2001, Brand had tried to drag her into the office bathroom for sex, becoming a “wild-eyed maniac,” in her words. (Brand was found not guilty on this charge.) Another complainant stated that Brand had squeezed her breasts and kissed her in broad view of his entourage while she was working at the radio station Choice FM in the mid-2000s, a charge on which he was convicted

A woman working for the British national TV broadcaster Channel 4 in 2009 testified that Brand had refused to film one day unless she gave him a massage, and when she’d acquiesced, he’d buried his face in her crotch while two of his associates watched and laughed. (Brand was also found guilty of this charge.) In court, Brand’s accusers were asked whether they’d told anyone else what had happened to them at the time (yes, they had told colleagues, two out of three of the above women said), and what had happened in response (nothing)

The line of questioning was perhaps necessary in a court of law but seemed ironic given that Brand’s entire career throughout the 2000s was built on transgressions very like the ones detailed in court, broadcast as national entertainment. [ Read: The unspeakable, enabled ] It’s easy to forget, deep into Brand’s third and fourth professional reincarnations as an online conspiracy theorist and an evangelist, that he became famous for relentless provocation
His persona—a mix of lolloping Dickensian scoundrel, glam-rock dandy, and grinning sexual deviant—was unique when he broke out as a comic in 2000
In a moment when the cheerful sexism of 1990s British culture was edging toward a darker mode, Brand’s willingness to violate every moral and social code was the core of his identity
In 2001, the day after 9/11, he was fired by MTV after showing up to work dressed as Osama bin Laden, with his own drug dealer in tow

In 2002, he filmed scenes for his satellite-TV show, Re:Brand , during which he took baths with an unhoused person and masturbated a man in a pub bathroom. (In his defense, he later specified, he was on crack and heroin at the time.) That year, Brand was also fired from his XFM radio show for reading pornographic material on the air
But every time he lost a job, he gained a better and more prestigious one

One woman testified in court that at a party in Soho in 2004—the same year that Brand was hired for his most high-profile gig yet, as the host of a show spun off from the smash reality series Big Brother —he’d grabbed her breasts and forced his penis into her mouth ( he was convicted of only the former act)

In 2006, the same year that he began hosting a BBC Radio Six show, Brand asked the TV presenter Vanessa Feltz, on another of his shows, whether he could “have it off” with her daughters, and harassed the singer Dannii Minogue so committedly that she described him as a “vile predator” who “wouldn’t take no for an answer.” All of this—the ritualistic diminishment of women doing their jobs, the ironic cruelty, the swaggering priapism—was so much a part of Brand’s schtick that it must have been what producers and commissioners liked about him

British culture was deeply confused about sex at the time: The waning anxiety of the AIDS era and the nascent force of the internet meant that sexual imagery was suddenly everywhere, and no one seemed to know the rules anymore

As a teenager in 1999, just home from school, I watched the pop stars Geri Halliwell and Kylie Minogue arm-wrestle and then make out on camera for the Channel 4 series TFI Friday , while the host, Chris Evans, cheered them on and replayed the footage, eyes darting out of his head like a cartoon coyote

In 2008, the BBC TV presenter Jonathan Ross simply told Gwyneth Paltrow on his talk show that he “ would fuck her .” Brand could only have emerged in this postfeminist moment, when people were still sanguine about objectifying women for sport, and not yet jaded by the extremities of the internet
What do people commonly do when they’re shocked? They laugh

Brand’s body of comedic work is made up of so many offenses, detailed by Brand himself in baroque and head-spinning verbiage, that to try to take stock of them all now feels like trying to compile the dictionary

In his 2007 memoir, My Booky Wook (supposedly titled after the Nadsat dialect spoken by the rapist marauders in A Clockwork Orange ), Brand describes, during high school, badgering a teenage girl named Penny for sex: “I painted verbal pictures and begged until she kissed me, I lied and danced and evoked the spirit of Pan till reluctantly she removed her bra, I used tears and emotional blackmail to secure the immolation of her knickers.” [ Read: No, women aren’t the problem ] Early in the days of his BBC radio show, Brand called a female newscaster “erotic,” saying , “We’re going to get under that desk and we’re gonna unleash hell on your thighs, woman.” (The woman complained to colleagues, causing Brand to further mock her on the air. “The producer just told me that we’ve upset her,” he said on another show. “They go, ‘She ain’t got the right to reply.’”) To Piers Morgan, in a 2006 GQ interview , Brand said that although he’d likely slept with close to 2,000 women, “I resent the word ‘predator.’ I like to think of myself as a conduit of natural forces

After all, the most natural thing in the world for people to do is f*, isn’t it? And people want to do it, so all you have to do is remove all the reasons why women don’t actually go through with it.” Brand’s defense lawyers, and his own testimony in court, maintained throughout that although he’d been an admitted—and eventually repentant—philanderer during the height of his fame, he had never had sex with a woman without her consent
The judge said yesterday that Brand will likely face “significant” time in prison, given the gravity of the offenses of which he was found guilty

It’s notable that in the years following 2010, as Brand’s acting roles puttered out and rumors circulated about what he was like to work with, he had to constantly reinvent himself to try to keep people’s attention

But his role at the beginning of the 21st century as the glinty-eyed, chaotic, intensely self-obsessed purveyor of sexual discomfort made him a mascot for his era, and he was enabled by far more people than will ever admit to it. “There was a culture of fear,” one of the complainants said in court about Channel 4, her workplace when Brand assaulted her. “Russell Brand was an A-lister star, it was Big Brother , people were watching it, we all watched it.”

title: Trump Doubles Down With Miller
excerpt: Introspection has never been one of Donald Trump’s more notable attributes
body: Introspection has never been one of Donald Trump’s more notable attributes
He never accepts blame or course-corrects; he only becomes a more distilled version of himself
And so, faced with rejection at the ballot box on an overwhelming scale, the president responded by replacing his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with Stephen Miller
Technically speaking, Miller had been Wiles’s second in command, as deputy chief of staff
In reality, Miller was already the administration’s most powerful figure, arguably including Trump himself

Steve Bannon, a former Trump adviser and a Miller ally who was briefly cast as the power behind the throne during Trump’s first term, described Miller earlier this year as Trump’s “prime minister.” In a parliamentary system, the president or monarch is merely the symbolic head of state, whereas the prime minister is the head of government
Wiles, though reputed for her professionalism and competence, held her job for nearly two years by facilitating Trump’s impulses without questioning them
Miller, however, has driven and shaped those impulses

Miller has repeatedly described the opposition as illegitimate. “The Democrat Party is not a political party,” he said last year. “It is a domestic extremist organization.” He has obsessively, and effectively, employed executive actions to circumvent Congress as a lawmaking body
Trump had little use for the legislature even when his allies controlled it
If Miller remains true to form, he will extend his reliance on executive action, and commit the administration to total defiance of any oversight
He is especially driven by his belief that immigration is a plot directed by left-wing elites to destroy traditional America
Miller, more than any other single factor, explains Trump’s baffling choice to blow up his 2024 coalition, which registered shocking gains among Latinos
He has directed the administration’s frantic campaign of mass deportation, acting in the belief that the GOP has four years to permanently reshape American demography or face permanent extinction
Miller, more than any other person, is responsible for unleashing violent havoc on American streets, as masked agents in unmarked vehicles have swept up suspects
He has also virtually shut down legal immigration—except for white South Africans, whom the administration has ostentatiously welcomed
Even Trump, according to The Wall Street Journal , has sometimes complained that Miller’s immigration enforcement has gone too far
Miller’s enforcement regimen is obviously not the sole cause of Trump’s unpopularity
Trump’s tariffs, corruption, cuts to health care, obsession with erecting monuments to or renaming them for himself, and the war with Iran all contributed to the disintegration of his coalition
Vance laid all of the blame on the war, absolving every other failure, it sent a signal that the administration would tolerate criticism only in this one, single realm
The signal sent by Miller’s elevation takes that message to the next step
Miller pitched himself to Trump as an advocate of winding down the war with Iran, The New York Times ’ Maggie Haberman reported
His elevation thus combines retreat on a single front—a front many Trump devotees regard as a betrayal of his “America First” principles—with a determination to advance on every other
Trump dwells in a zero-sum world, divided between winners and losers
His instinct in a moment of defeat is to empower an aide who he himself recognizes has at times gone too far
But Trump cannot admit he has failed, or bring himself to show any weakness
Better to go too far than not far enough.

title: The Education a STEM Major Needs
excerpt: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books
body: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books
In 2014, I graduated from college with a dubious degree: I majored in English, a discipline that, in a time of growing STEM mania, was widely considered a relic of questionable value
At the end of my studies, my adviser asked me what I’d taken away from the program
I had spent enough time examining the minds of brilliant others—learning how they chose words, built characters, and developed ideas—to feel some mastery over my own

In a new Atlantic essay , Joshua Bennett, a literature professor at MIT, makes the case that such an education should be foundational for all students, including and perhaps especially those focusing on science
First, here are six new stories from The Atlantic ’s Books section: Six books you should read twice He was hugely influential

The golden age of hockey literature What if the apocalypse is already here? “The Toll,” a poem by Forrest Gander Bennett’s students have grown up in a society defined by rapid technological growth; some of them likely dream of building a world we can’t imagine today, especially now that new AI technologies are pushing the frontier of the possible
At the same time, the state of the humanities has become even more fragile than it was during my undergraduate career
Humanities departments across the country are being squeezed or shut down entirely
Too many students have never been assigned the once-standard task of reading a whole book
The number of undergraduate humanities degrees awarded by American universities in 2025 was nearly a third lower than it was in 2012, although the decline might be approaching a plateau

That crisis is part of what’s driving Bennett and some of his colleagues to design a Great Books course for MIT, the kind of sweeping introduction to canonical, time-tested literature and philosophy that helps anchor many liberal-arts educations

Given the students he’s working with, Bennett’s program will focus on “the history, poetics, and philosophy of science.” A solid grounding in the humanities, he argues, is essential to the intellectual development of future scientists, in part because it can help them “identify irreplaceable ideas during a time of accelerated change.” The possibility of an imminent techno-utopia, in which work is automated and life is easy—or, conversely, a tech-driven apocalypse, in which human inventions come to subjugate humanity—makes it ever more important to teach students how to engage deeply with the age-old query: What is life for? Studying the plays of the ancient Greeks or the logical puzzles of Kant won’t, of course, provide a single answer

But doing so can help teach students how to think about the problem—to wonder, What is the meaning of life? as well as, What distinguishes a thoughtful idea from a shallow truism? To ask more questions, and to pursue the answers with rigor, is to open more routes toward meaning
Bennett’s “irreplaceable ideas” are not formulas to memorize; they’re vigorous, adaptable entities
You cannot learn, once and for all, what they mean
You can only build the habit of thinking about them for yourself
The Time Is Right for a ‘Great Books’ Revival By Joshua Bennett To build a better world in the age of AI, students need grounding in indispensable ideas

What to Read The Perfectionists , by Simon Winchester The Perfectionists dramatically explores the history of engineers figuring out how to manufacture things—mostly out of metal, glass and other hard materials—into exacting shapes and sizes, making possible our world of cars, jet engines, and microprocessor chips
The story begins, and is intimately bound up, with the Industrial Revolution

John Wilkinson, one of the fathers of precision engineering, devised snug-fitting cylinders for James Watt’s steam engine, and the early days of the discipline are similarly full of delightfully specific historical objects: pulleys made for British naval ships, for example, and the fiddly bits of flintlock muskets

But as Winchester steps through the great advancements that pushed this school of engineering to new extremes, he makes clear that we now rely on machines to achieve a perfection unattainable by people, and that this comes with hefty stakes

An improperly machined oil pipe, for instance, caused catastrophic engine failure on a 2010 Qantas flight because it was “about half a millimeter too thin,” he writes. (Thanks to an experienced crew, everyone on board survived.) Perhaps, he suggests, a deeper respect for imperfect human craftsmanship might live alongside our reverence for mechanical technique. — Chelsea Leu From our list: Eight books that explain how the world works Out Next Week 📚 The Land of Tears and Hope: The Ukrainian Story , by Illia Ponomarenko 📚 Vocal Break: On Women, Music, and Power , by Lauren Elkin 📚 No Such Thing as Monday: A Novel , by Siân Hughes Your Weekend Read Ian Loring Shiver and Minnie Park for The Atlantic The Rise of the Tallboy Is a Sign of the Times By Megan Garber Say you’re at a football game (fun!), in large part for the food (correct!)

You have spent your time at the stadium successfully curating an alfresco fine-dining experience: the pregame amuse-bouche (popcorn, maybe, with a swirl of let’s-agree-to-call-it-butter), the first-quarter aperitif (a frosty can of beer), the second-quarter appetizer (a plate of fries, doused with ketchup), the third-quarter entrée (nachos, obviously, washed down with a second beer)
It’s now the fourth quarter, and although the game has gone as planned (probably? you haven’t been paying tons of attention), your dessert course has not
The menu options before you—churro, cotton candy—are leaving you stymied
That is possibly because, you come to realize, you are unexpectedly drunk

excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Data centers, megadonors, and corruption had a bad Election Night
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Data centers, megadonors, and corruption had a bad Election Night
Prediction markets did just fine, but were a bit overhyped

So will the midterm results change how tech leaders move forward? What will a Democratic Congress mean for their businesses? In this episode, Charlie Warzel gets into what this election changes for the tech world, how voters saw through AI ads and billionaire donors, and whether we’re moving into a post–Elon Musk political era
The following is a transcript of the episode: Mike Isaac: I feel like there’s such intense pushback on the data centers specifically
And this is not a new idea, but like it really is this physical manifestation of economic insecurity; that fighting against AI in the ether is much harder to do

But if you’re like, No, this is a giant cube that I hate, that is in my backyard, that represents my doom ultimately —yeah, that’s kind of a layup in a lot of ways, you know? Charlie Warzel: It’s just a national pain sponge, right? Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain
You may have noticed there was an election on Tuesday night
Millions of dollars flooded into prediction markets
People across the country cast ballots on data-center initiatives, and they told surveyors and exit polls how they felt about megadonors, corruption, and artificial intelligence
One of the big stories of the last few years is the way that many tech leaders and investors have aligned themselves with Donald Trump in his second term
It’s an issue that’s polarized Silicon Valley, and in very important ways, changed the trajectory of technologies like AI and crypto
And on Tuesday night, we learned a lot about how Americans feel about that realignment and about the influence that some of Silicon Valley’s richest people have in our politics
We also got a chance to see how AI, prediction markets, and tech money shaped or didn’t shape electoral outcomes
And so today on Galaxy Brain , we are breaking down what the midterms meant for the tech world

Did prediction markets win the night? Was this the AI election? What happens next for Elon Musk, for the companies who bent the knee to Trump, for the AI labs? We’re taping this on Wednesday right after the midterms, and we’re going to be splitting this conversation up into two conversations
First, I’ll be talking with Mike Isaac, who has covered Silicon Valley for The New York Times for over a decade, and in December he’ll be writing about all of it for us here at The Atlantic
Then I’m going to talk about prediction markets with Will Gottsegen
He’s my colleague who writes the Over/Under newsletter for The Atlantic , which covers risk and prediction markets
Mike Isaac joins me to talk about it now. [ Music ] Warzel: Mike Isaac, my future colleague, welcome to Galaxy Brain
Warzel: What was, in your mind, the biggest story of the night in tech? Isaac: I mean, personally the biggest story was it feeling like 2014 Twitter vibes again to me
My favorite—this was just very funny culturally—was like, I saw this term come up: I’m not doomscrolling; I’m hopescrolling , a lot of people have been saying
Which is like, you know, obviously a huge wipeout for Republicans across the board, I think

But as far as Techland goes, you know, there was a very clear referendum across I wanna say 40-something ballots—that data centers and this sort of inexorable trudge of AI into everyone’s towns is getting held up
You know, is getting pushed back by a lot of voters

And I think folks in the Valley, at least the ones that I’ve been talking to so far, have been kinda trying to reckon with that and say, Okay, how do we change our positions? I think what they’ll do—I think what the companies will do—is be like, It’s a messaging issue
All they’ve heard from us has been doom and gloom

You know, certain companies are like, Dario Amodei over at Anthropic is really screwing us, because all he does is talk about how this is gonna destroy the world and take our jobs, but we need to do it
And so my guess is that they’ll try to massage the messaging and say: Here’s, you know, drug discovery
Here’s ways that AI can improve the world
You need to learn how to have it augment your job rather than replace you entirely
But I think that, you know, it’s always gonna come back to that
Because fundamentally there are people who just think it’s not good for the world—developing this technology, certain versions of this technology, is not good for the world
And I think that doesn’t square with a lot of the worldviews among some camps in Silicon Valley who do think it’s just an unmitigated good, no matter how many rocky patches we go through

Like, how do you wrestle with that on a fundamental level, on a human level, when people are repudiating everything you’re trying to do, you know? Warzel: I’m curious; there was some debate going into this, like, you know, This is gonna be the AI election
And then there was I believe our mutual friend Casey Newton argued in his newsletter Platformer last week that this would not be the AI election
And some of that was like, voter anxieties were—economic concerns were much more a factor than something like AI and data centers
Turns out maybe that wasn’t necessarily true
But also I think what Casey was referring to is the idea that people were worried about a lot of AI deepfakes or, you know, potential misinformation
Or chatbots leading people to different canonical answers about who to vote for, or whatnot
And I’m just curious: In your mind, was this the “AI election”? How should we be framing that? Isaac: That’s a really good point

title: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
excerpt: A robot cleaned my apartment for $30 — San Francisco startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots into people's homes, piloted remotely by humans who co
body: A robot cleaned my apartment for $30 — San Francisco startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots into people's homes, piloted remotely by humans who collect training data while the robots clean — making the service cheaper than you'd expect for something this futuristic
Cute but clumsy — The four-and-a-half-foot robot climbed stairs like it was drunk, knocked over olive oil, and left taps dripping — but impressively reattached its toilet brush wand three times

The Jetsons, with caveats — If autonomous cleaning robots become real, the human cost could be steep: cleaning workers could lose their jobs, and U.S. policy is nowhere near ready to handle that. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148090" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner
I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser
But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist
I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons , even if just for an hour
I was also motivated by journalistic interest
In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up

Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists
As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants
Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round
Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product
At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit
But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain

They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.  But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute

Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks)
Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors
With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos

Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them
These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data
Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there

But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help

If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide
The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle
It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee
That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door
I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps
Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing

When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said
Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps

As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment

Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she says that’s no longer necessary.) You can’t fault Tau on customer service, though
Weinzierl quickly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist

I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger
In the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet

That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle
The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta
It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled
But I easily forgave all those missteps because of how charming it was
As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out

title: Pope Leo’s trip is a homecoming to Peru – where debate over liberation theology roiled the church during his early years as a priest

<title>Pope Leo’s trip is a homecoming to Peru – where debate over liberation theology roiled the church during his early years as a priest</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770403/original/file-20261105-64-909jxl.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7102%2C4734&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A mototaxi drives past a banner of Pope Leo XIV in Chiclayo, Peru, on Nov. 5, 2026, ahead of his trip to Latin America.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/PeruPope/7296c0075d304da7a2ef4351555684f7/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=pope%20leo&amp;currentItemNo=2&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Martin Mejia</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Pope Leo XIV travels to Latin America on Nov. 6, 2026, with <a href="https://press.vatican.va/content/salastampa/it/bollettino/pubblico/2026/09/21/0736/01738.html#en">a packed itinerary</a> that will bring him through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It is Leo’s first trip to the region since his elevation to the papacy – and a homecoming for <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-pope-is-peruvian-how-2-decades-in-south-america-shaped-the-vision-of-pope-leo-xiv-256415">a pope who spent two decades in Peru</a> and holds Peruvian citizenship.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://www.rit.edu/directory/eblgla-eben-levey">a historian</a> of <a href="https://doi.org/10.13016/4bla-77sh">Catholicism in the late 20th century</a>, I couldn’t help but notice that <a href="https://press.vatican.va/content/salastampa/it/bollettino/pubblico/2026/09/21/0736/01738.html">the pope’s plans</a> walk a fine line during a fraught political moment in Latin America.</p>

<p>Leo plans to meet with the <a href="https://en.mercopress.com/2026/11/03/the-pope-arrives-in-an-argentina-where-bishops-are-among-milei-s-firmest-critics">right-wing presidents of Argentina</a> <a href="https://www.ncronline.org/vatican/vatican-news/pope-leos-latin-america-trip-high-stakes-homecoming">and Peru</a>. He will also visit sites often associated with the progressive wing of the Catholic Church, including Casavalle, one of the <a href="https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20261101-seen-and-heard-uruguay-neighborhood-places-hopes-in-pope">poorest neighborhoods</a> in Uruguay’s capital. In Argentina, where President Javier Milei has <a href="https://apnews.com/article/argentina-javier-milei-trump-disabilities-austerity-6d98fb3cecc91fe4f3e3f8800826275e">drastically cut</a> funding for disability services, the pope will go to a Catholic home for disabled people.</p>

<p>And in Chiclayo, Peru, where Leo served as a bishop, he will pray at a chapel dedicated to St. Óscar Romero. A Salvadoran archbishop, Romero <a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/assassination-of-a-saint/paper">was assassinated in 1980</a> after years of speaking out against the human rights violations committed by the <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/36700/the-massacre-at-el-mozote-by-mark-danner/">U.S.-supported</a> <a href="https://www.calmigration.org/learn-chapter/civil-war">Salvadoran military</a>. His ministry was influenced by <a href="https://theconversation.com/after-50-years-liberation-theology-is-still-reshaping-catholicism-and-politics-but-what-is-it-186804">liberation theology</a>, a controversial movement born in Peru that roiled church politics for decades – including during Leo’s years in Peru.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770404/original/file-20261105-64-hzvkma.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A close-up photo of someone's two cupped hands, holding a gold and silver ornament with a picture of a priest with glasses." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770404/original/file-20261105-64-hzvkma.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770404/original/file-20261105-64-hzvkma.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770404/original/file-20261105-64-hzvkma.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770404/original/file-20261105-64-hzvkma.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770404/original/file-20261105-64-hzvkma.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770404/original/file-20261105-64-hzvkma.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770404/original/file-20261105-64-hzvkma.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">An ornament features St. Oscar Romero during a religious procession honoring him in San Salvador, El Salvador, on Aug. 1, 2024.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/ElSalvadorSaintRomero/74cc3a03a6ad4cbb942f342096b84e44/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=oscar%20romero&amp;currentItemNo=21&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Salvador Melendez</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What is liberation theology?</h2>

<p>The name itself was coined in a 1968 lecture by <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/23/world/americas/gustavo-gutierrez-dead.html">Gustavo Gutiérrez</a>, a Peruvian theologian and priest. He expanded on his ideas in a 1971 book, “<a href="https://orbisbooks.com/products/9781626985414?srsltid=AYCX9vIJkIEBTafm65WkZiA2WWXGZFkSkEwMIPHf0HdvB5Xz2kRYparw">A Theology of Liberation</a>.” </p>

<p>Gutiérrez and like-minded theologians argued that Christians have a moral duty <a href="https://theconversation.com/after-50-years-liberation-theology-is-still-reshaping-catholicism-and-politics-but-what-is-it-186804">to liberate the oppressed</a>. They saw poverty, violence, racism and discrimination as not just problems but collective sins. While building on earlier Catholic social teachings, these “liberationists” envisioned profound change that went beyond the spiritual care and charitable work of traditional Latin American Catholicism. </p>

<p>Catholics <a href="https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/E/bo3631145.html">inspired by liberation theology</a> created community organizations and work cooperatives, organized labor unions and fostered other initiatives that sought to measurably improve the lives of the poor. In <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/liberation-theology-and-the-others-9781793633637/">my own research</a>, I’ve documented how priests and nuns in rural Mexico helped organize transportation, corn milling and carpentry cooperatives.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770405/original/file-20261105-64-4e1iix.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A black and white photo of a man in a sweater, collarded shirt and glasses holding up his finger as he speaks." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770405/original/file-20261105-64-4e1iix.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770405/original/file-20261105-64-4e1iix.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=863&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770405/original/file-20261105-64-4e1iix.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=863&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770405/original/file-20261105-64-4e1iix.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=863&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770405/original/file-20261105-64-4e1iix.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1084&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770405/original/file-20261105-64-4e1iix.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1084&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770405/original/file-20261105-64-4e1iix.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1084&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Gustavo Gutiérrez’s writings provided the foundation for liberation theology in the 1960s and ’70s.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/gustavo-gutierrez-founder-of-liberation-theology-said-in-an-news-photo/515505054?phrase=gustavo%20gutierrez%20priest&amp;adppopup=true">Bettmann/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Gutiérrez also argued that Christians should use Marxist ideas about <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/pedagogy-of-the-oppressed-9781501314131/">analyzing society and the economy</a> to <a href="https://monthlyreview.org/9780853450931/">better understand inequality</a>. In nations like Peru, <a href="https://doi.org/10.4324/9780429315060">which possessed rich natural resources</a>, liberationists tailored their economic justice projects to address how international and national companies profited off the low wages of miners and farmers.</p>

<p>During the Cold War, however, these ideas led some politicians and church leaders to accuse liberationists of socialism and communism.</p>

<p>A minority fringe of liberationists did embrace left-ring radicalism. <a href="https://kellogg.nd.edu/space-utopia-christians-socialism-chile">Christians for Socialism</a>, for example, argued that liberation <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/blog/2025/12/12/the-chilean-christians-for-socialism-movement-liberationist-third-worldist-and-utopian/">meant rejecting capitalism</a>. Some clergy, although only a handful, even <a href="https://www.routledge.com/Camilo-Torres-Priest-Liberation-Theologian-Guerrilla-Fighter/Ginzberg/p/book/9781032990255">picked up arms</a> to fight alongside clandestine left-wing revolutionary groups. </p>

<h2>A wary pope</h2>

<p>This presented a dilemma to the Vatican. </p>

<p>In 1891, Pope Leo XIII – <a href="https://theconversation.com/19th-century-catholic-teachings-21st-century-tech-how-concerns-about-ai-guided-pope-leos-choice-of-name-256645">the current pope’s namesake</a> – <a href="https://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiii/en/encyclicals/documents/hf_l-xiii_enc_15051891_rerum-novarum.html">published “Rerum Novarum</a>,” an encyclical focused on workers’ rights amid the Industrial Revolution. Since then, the Vatican had critiqued the worst excesses of capitalism while also rejecting socialism and communism, which it viewed as godless ideologies. </p>

<p>During the 1960s and ’70s, Pope Paul VI generally <a href="https://www.commonwealmagazine.org/introduction-%E2%80%98commonweal%E2%80%99-and-liberation-theology">supported local initiatives by liberationist Catholics</a>, including some <a href="https://www.nybooks.com/online/2026/05/24/the-education-of-pope-leo-xiv/">in Chulucanas, Peru</a>, where Leo began his missionary work. Paul appointed and elevated bishops who shared a vision that the church could help empower the poor and alleviate oppression. </p>

<p>But the Vatican shifted when the Polish cardinal Karol Józef Wojtyla became Pope John Paul II in 1978. For most of his adult life, Poland had been part of the Soviet bloc, which imposed restrictions on organized religion. A <a href="https://www.anneapplebaum.com/2005/04/06/how-the-pope-defeated-communism/">staunch opponent of communism</a>, <a href="https://time.com/archive/6854086/religion-john-paul-vs-liberation-theology/">he worried about liberation theology’s</a> use of Marxist analysis. So did one of his top Vatican officials, Joseph Ratzinger – the future Pope Benedict XVI.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770406/original/file-20261105-64-ei7hcy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man in white vestments kneels in the grass in front of a slab of stone while a crowd of people look on." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770406/original/file-20261105-64-ei7hcy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770406/original/file-20261105-64-ei7hcy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770406/original/file-20261105-64-ei7hcy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770406/original/file-20261105-64-ei7hcy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770406/original/file-20261105-64-ei7hcy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770406/original/file-20261105-64-ei7hcy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770406/original/file-20261105-64-ei7hcy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Pope John Paul II prays at the tomb of anti-communist dissident priest Jerzy Popieluszko, in front of the Church of St. Stanislas in Warsaw, on June 14, 1987.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/pope-john-paul-ii-prays-14-june-1987-in-warsaw-in-front-of-news-photo/136742376?phrase=%22john%20paul%22%20communism&amp;adppopup=true">Jean-Claude Delmas/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The Vatican began investigating <a href="https://wipfandstock.com/products/marx-and-the-bible-9781592444854?srsltid=AYCX9vK51gjTntA4LFREX5-quPazIhRZj3zxLHw_WdGvf0hAHqxu3p6B">some liberation theologians</a> for violations of church teachings. In 1985, for example, Brazilian liberationist theologian Leonardo Boff was ordered to observe a <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/813628776">year of silence</a> – no publishing, no public speaking – to discipline him for his critique of the church’s hierarchy. Several priests <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-latin-america-28656661">were suspended</a> <a href="https://www.americamagazine.org/news/2016/02/23/nicaragua-jesuit-fernando-cardenal-dies-82/">over their work</a> in Sandinista Nicaragua.</p>

<p>John Paul ordered that the Peruvian bishops begin an investigation of Gutiérrez – above all, over <a href="https://www.ncronline.org/news/theology/vatican-doctrinal-czar-liberation-theology-pioneer-reflects-troubles">Marxism’s influence on his work</a>. Gutiérrez was ultimately not punished. </p>

<p>One factor in his favor may have been his consistent opposition to armed revolution, even before violence raged in Peru from the 1980s into the ’90s. <a href="https://www.dukeupress.edu/Shining-and-Other-Paths">The Shining Path</a>, a Maoist guerrilla group, was waging a war of terrorism against the Peruvian government, setting off bombs across Peru. </p>

<p>Under President Alberto Fujimori, the government escalated existing counterinsurgency operations, often using indiscriminate violence against citizens in the region where the Shining Path emerged. In 2009, Fujimori was convicted of <a href="https://academic.oup.com/ijtj/article-abstract/3/3/384/2888395?redirectedFrom=fulltext">human rights violations</a>.</p>

<h2>Young priest</h2>

<p>Leo has never described himself as a liberationist Catholic. However, his experiences as a priest were <a href="https://www.nybooks.com/online/2026/05/24/the-education-of-pope-leo-xiv/">indelibly shaped by liberation theology</a>, the Peruvian armed conflict and the church debates that roiled much of Latin America during his years there.</p>

<p>Leo, born Robert Prevost, was raised in Chicago. After ordination, his journey as a priest began in Peru, where he landed for missionary work in 1985. The young friar followed in the footsteps of other <a href="https://undpress.nd.edu/9780268029050/maryknoll-catholic-mission-in-peru-1943-1989/">U.S. Catholic missionaries</a> who had been serving among Peru’s poor and Indigenous, urban and rural, since the 1940s.</p>

<figure class="align-left zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770408/original/file-20261105-64-8u2bf4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A black and white portrait of a man with dark hair in a suit and tie." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770408/original/file-20261105-64-8u2bf4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770408/original/file-20261105-64-8u2bf4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=790&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770408/original/file-20261105-64-8u2bf4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=790&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770408/original/file-20261105-64-8u2bf4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=790&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770408/original/file-20261105-64-8u2bf4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=993&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770408/original/file-20261105-64-8u2bf4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=993&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770408/original/file-20261105-64-8u2bf4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=993&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Sent to Chulucanas, in Peru’s coastal northwest, Prevost found himself in a region of pastoral experimentation. Since the 1960s, Augustinian missionaries had been <a href="https://www.nybooks.com/online/2026/05/24/the-education-of-pope-leo-xiv/">working closely</a> with the community to provide literacy education, discussion groups about poverty and inequality, and workshops to train artisans. </p>

<p>These programs were a far cry from the more radical actions of some Catholics who supported liberation theology. Nevertheless, the programs in Chulucanas aimed to empower the Peruvian poor, chipping away at exploitation and low wages on the region’s sugarcane and cotton estates. Like Gutiérrez, many Peruvian Christians believed that the Shining Path <a href="https://doi.org/10.1179/1462317X13Z.0000000004">drew support because of pervasive poverty and inequality</a>, and that churches could help transform the nation. </p>

<p>But the Catholic Church in Latin America was in the midst of another transformation. John Paul gradually appointed <a href="https://www.routledge.com/The-Politics-of-Transnational-Actors-in-Latin-America-Power-from-Afar/Shepherd/p/book/9781138096332">conservative bishops</a> across the continent. Experimental pastoral programs lost support, and institutions that trained priests to put liberation theology into action, such as the <a href="https://doi.org/10.13016/4bla-77sh">Regional Seminary of the Southeast</a> in Mexico, were shuttered or “reoriented.” </p>

<p>Yet even as the hierarchy shifted conservative, work on the ground among Latin America’s poorest continued apace. From <a href="https://press.umich.edu/Books/D/Divined-Intervention2">coffee cooperatives in Mexico</a> to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1515/9783111726069">human rights activists</a> across the continent, many programs survived.</p>

<h2>‘Cease the repression’</h2>

<p>Leo’s 2026 itinerary includes multiple stops that speak to this history and on-the-ground pastoral work. The most symbolic, perhaps, is the Capilla San Óscar Romero, located in Chiclayo, the pope’s former diocese.</p>

<p>A neighborhood chapel <a href="https://www.latintimes.com/pope-leo-xiv-visit-chiclayo-chapel-600527">renovated with donations</a> from Leo’s connections in the United States, it is one of many sites throughout the Americas honoring Catholics who fell victim to right-wing, anti-communist violence. The day before Romero’s assassination, he used his weekly radio address to speak directly to El Salvador’s conscripted soldiers, telling them, “<a href="https://sojo.net/magazine/may-1980/pastors-last-homily">No soldier is obliged to obey an order counter to the law of God</a>.”</p>

<p>Leo XIV’s visit to the chapel is for private prayer, not a homily or a speech. Still, I would argue that the soft-spoken pope’s stop will evoke Romero’s message – especially at a time of <a href="https://apnews.com/article/rubio-peru-drug-trafficking-trump-b625fe79a901799707343ff5dd83b5f4">strikes against suspected drug traffickers</a>, which <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2025/09/18/us-maritime-strikes-amount-to-extrajudicial-killings">human rights groups</a> have <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/ck5ye7v88qy7o">criticized as extrajudicial killings</a>. <a href="https://sojo.net/magazine/may-1980/pastors-last-homily">During his final Mass</a>, Romero pleaded, “I beseech you, I beg you, I command you in the name of God: Cease the repression!”</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294299/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

AP Photo/Martin Mejia Pope Leo XIV travels to Latin America on Nov. 6, 2026, with a packed itinerary that will bring him through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru
It is Leo’s first trip to the region since his elevation to the papacy – and a homecoming for a pope who spent two decades in Peru and holds Peruvian citizenship
As a historian of Catholicism in the late 20th century , I couldn’t help but notice that the pope’s plans walk a fine line during a fraught political moment in Latin America
Leo plans to meet with the right-wing presidents of Argentina and Peru
He will also visit sites often associated with the progressive wing of the Catholic Church, including Casavalle, one of the poorest neighborhoods in Uruguay’s capital
In Argentina, where President Javier Milei has drastically cut funding for disability services, the pope will go to a Catholic home for disabled people
And in Chiclayo, Peru, where Leo served as a bishop, he will pray at a chapel dedicated to St. Óscar Romero
A Salvadoran archbishop, Romero was assassinated in 1980 after years of speaking out against the human rights violations committed by the U.S.-supported Salvadoran military
His ministry was influenced by liberation theology , a controversial movement born in Peru that roiled church politics for decades – including during Leo’s years in Peru
Oscar Romero during a religious procession honoring him in San Salvador, El Salvador, on Aug. 1, 2024
AP Photo/Salvador Melendez What is liberation theology? The name itself was coined in a 1968 lecture by Gustavo Gutiérrez , a Peruvian theologian and priest
He expanded on his ideas in a 1971 book, “ A Theology of Liberation .” Gutiérrez and like-minded theologians argued that Christians have a moral duty to liberate the oppressed
They saw poverty, violence, racism and discrimination as not just problems but collective sins

While building on earlier Catholic social teachings, these “liberationists” envisioned profound change that went beyond the spiritual care and charitable work of traditional Latin American Catholicism

Catholics inspired by liberation theology created community organizations and work cooperatives, organized labor unions and fostered other initiatives that sought to measurably improve the lives of the poor
In my own research , I’ve documented how priests and nuns in rural Mexico helped organize transportation, corn milling and carpentry cooperatives
Gustavo Gutiérrez’s writings provided the foundation for liberation theology in the 1960s and ’70s
Bettmann/Getty Images Gutiérrez also argued that Christians should use Marxist ideas about analyzing society and the economy to better understand inequality

In nations like Peru, which possessed rich natural resources , liberationists tailored their economic justice projects to address how international and national companies profited off the low wages of miners and farmers
During the Cold War, however, these ideas led some politicians and church leaders to accuse liberationists of socialism and communism
A minority fringe of liberationists did embrace left-ring radicalism
Christians for Socialism , for example, argued that liberation meant rejecting capitalism
Some clergy, although only a handful, even picked up arms to fight alongside clandestine left-wing revolutionary groups
A wary pope This presented a dilemma to the Vatican
In 1891, Pope Leo XIII – the current pope’s namesake – published “Rerum Novarum ,” an encyclical focused on workers’ rights amid the Industrial Revolution
Since then, the Vatican had critiqued the worst excesses of capitalism while also rejecting socialism and communism, which it viewed as godless ideologies
During the 1960s and ’70s, Pope Paul VI generally supported local initiatives by liberationist Catholics , including some in Chulucanas, Peru , where Leo began his missionary work
Paul appointed and elevated bishops who shared a vision that the church could help empower the poor and alleviate oppression
But the Vatican shifted when the Polish cardinal Karol Józef Wojtyla became Pope John Paul II in 1978
For most of his adult life, Poland had been part of the Soviet bloc, which imposed restrictions on organized religion
A staunch opponent of communism , he worried about liberation theology’s use of Marxist analysis

<title>Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms stands on the shoulders of Stacey Abrams, Charlotta Bass and countless other Black women who dreamed</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770533/original/file-20261106-64-2n6ykk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3824%2C2549&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms hugs her daughter Lincoln during an election night watch party in Atlanta, Ga., on Nov. 3, 2026. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/georgia-gov-elect-keisha-lance-bottoms-hugs-her-daughter-news-photo/2303419319?phrase=keisha%20lance%20bottoms%20daughter&amp;adppopup=true">Megan Varner/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>There are elections that change the political map. And then there are elections that make you wonder whether the land itself remembers.</p>

<p>Georgia remembers.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/horrors-great-slave-auction-180962287/">The auction blocks</a>. <a href="https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/slavery-in-antebellum-georgia/">The cotton fields</a>. <a href="https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/lynching/">The lynching trees</a>. The Black women who cleaned governors’ homes but could not dream of becoming governor themselves.</p>

<p>And now Keisha Lance Bottoms has been elected <a href="https://apnews.com/article/georgia-governor-lance-bottom-jackson-midterm-election-67c22a38b9a6e4cad5584aa44acf106f">Georgia’s first Black woman governor</a>. The first Black woman elected governor of any American state.</p>

<p>Bottoms has <a href="https://www.ajc.com/politics/2026/11/keisha-lance-bottoms-crawfordville-governors-mansion/">traced her ancestry back five generations</a> to an enslaved person on a plantation near Crawfordville, Georgia. </p>

<p>An ancestor held in bondage on Georgia soil. A descendant elected to govern it.</p>

<p>The same earth. An entirely different claim to power. How many women had to believe in a future they would never live to see?</p>

<p>Bottoms’s victory represents the paradox of Black political advancement amid racial violence and the often-unrecognized labor of women who build futures they may never inhabit. Ultimately, Bottoms’ victory reflects both extraordinary progress and the unfinished work of American democracy. </p>



<h2>The children who deserved a future</h2>

<p>I keep thinking about the little children.</p>

<p>Between 1979 and 1981, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2019/04/30/us/atlanta-child-murders.html">Atlanta was terrorized</a> by the disappearances and murders of Black children and young adults. Mothers pleaded for answers. Families lived in a city where childhood itself had become dangerous.</p>

<p>The murders unfolded just years after <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1973/10/17/archives/atlanta-elects-a-black-mayor-first-in-a-major-southern-city-black.html">Maynard Jackson’s historic 1973 election</a> as Atlanta’s first Black mayor. His victory announced a new era of Black political power. Yet that power could not shield the city’s most vulnerable children. <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/2005/08/07/klan-was-probed-in-child-killings-in-atlanta/334ee8d7-5322-428a-9ebe-d05efaacf19b/">Suspicions of Ku Klux Klan involvement circulated</a>, although the Klan’s responsibility was never established.</p>

<p>That distinction matters. So does the fear.</p>

<p><a href="https://blackpast.org/african-american-history/keisha-lance-bottoms-1970/">Bottoms was born in 1970</a>. She was 9 when the murders began. She grew up in the same Atlanta where Black parents searched desperately for their missing children. She belonged to the generation whose futures were being stolen. And now she is preparing to lead the entire state.</p>

<p>What a terrible, beautiful, complicated thing.</p>

<p>Those murdered children were not symbols waiting to become useful to history. They were sons and daughters who deserved the ordinary miracle of growing older. They deserved a future. </p>

<p><a href="https://nul.org/basic-page/state-black-america-mayor-keisha-lance-bottoms">Bottoms later occupied the mayor’s office</a> that Jackson first opened to Black leadership. Now she is preparing to occupy the governor’s mansion. History has not erased its cruelty. But it has delivered an astonishing answer. </p>

<p>And this victory does not belong to Bottoms alone.</p>

<h2>The woman who sowed the seeds</h2>

<p>This victory belongs, in no small measure, to <a href="https://civilrightsmuseum.org/blog/stacey-abrams-champion-of-voting-rights-honored-at-the-national-civil-rights-museum/">democracy advocate, legislator and lawyer Stacey Abrams</a>. Perhaps those who recognize what Abrams made possible have sent her flowers. </p>

<p>Abrams ran for Georgia governor in 2018 and 2022. She <a href="https://atlanta.capitalbnews.org/abrams-loss-recap/">lost both races</a>. But through the <a href="https://slsvcoalition.org/partner/new-georgia-project/">New Georgia Project</a> and <a href="https://fairfight.com/">Fair Fight</a>, organizations focused on engaging voters and protecting voting rights, she helped build an electorate that could imagine Georgia differently. <a href="https://www.britannica.com/question/How-has-Stacey-Abrams-worked-to-protect-voting-rights">She registered voters, challenged barriers to participation</a>, and refused to accept that the South’s political future was fixed.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770531/original/file-20261106-64-v5o966.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A crowd of people holding signs and paying attention to someone not in the photo." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770531/original/file-20261106-64-v5o966.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/770531/original/file-20261106-64-v5o966.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770531/original/file-20261106-64-v5o966.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770531/original/file-20261106-64-v5o966.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770531/original/file-20261106-64-v5o966.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770531/original/file-20261106-64-v5o966.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/770531/original/file-20261106-64-v5o966.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Supporters listen as Democratic gubernatorial candidate Stacey Abrams speaks at a rally in Atlanta, Ga., on Nov. 5, 2022.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/democratic-supporters-listen-as-democratic-gubernatorial-news-photo/1244566907?phrase=stacey%20abrams%20crowd&amp;adppopup=true">Nathan Posner/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>And now another Black woman has won the office Abrams twice sought, in the third gubernatorial race in a row <a href="https://amsterdamnews.com/news/2026/11/03/keisha-lance-bottoms-wins-georgia-governor/">headed by a Black Democratic woman</a>. There is something biblical about the path Abrams steadfastly cleared. I think of Moses, guiding his people toward the Promised Land but never entering it himself. </p>

<p>Abrams’ journey is not over. Nor should her accomplishments be measured by another woman’s victory. But I believe there is sacred work in preparing a future you may never personally enjoy. Some people plant trees. Some people sit in their shade. Stacey Abrams planted. Bottoms is standing beneath the branches.</p>

<p>And as <a href="https://annenberg.usc.edu/faculty/allissa-v-richardson">a scholar of Black media history</a>, I can reach even further back, to another woman who understood the audacity of claiming political power: <a href="https://scetv.pbslearningmedia.org/resource/ull20-charlotta-spears-bass-video/unladylike2020/">Charlotta Bass</a>. </p>

<p>In 1952, Bass became <a href="https://www.womenshistory.org/education-resources/biographies/charlotta-spears-bass">the first Black woman nominated for vice president</a> of the United States, running on the Progressive Party ticket. </p>

<h2>The future Charlotta dared to imagine</h2>

<p>Before the <a href="https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/voting-rights-act">Voting Rights Act</a> in 1965, before <a href="https://naacp.org/find-resources/history-explained/1963-march-washington">the March on Washington</a> in 1963, before <a href="https://www.nps.gov/features/malu/feat0002/wof/Maynard_Jackson.htm">Jackson was elected mayor</a> in 1973 and before Abrams or Bottoms drew their first breaths, there was Bass. </p>

<p>A Black newspaper publisher who <a href="https://pdf.core.ac.uk/corefilesystem/pdf/3479/232565552.pdf?se=2026-11-06T14%3A49%3A25Z&amp;sp=r&amp;sv=2026-10-06&amp;sr=b&amp;rscd=inline%3B%20filename%3D%22232565552.pdf%22&amp;rsct=application/pdf&amp;sig=Y7M28jTj/2PaKi3HGTqRECrtsAL1wcvmVpZVSCC87xI%3D">confronted segregation, police brutality and white supremacist violence</a> in her four-decade ownership of <a href="https://www.pbs.org/blackpress/news_bios/ca_eagle.html">The California Eagle</a>, Bass understood that political power was about more than winning office. It was about who had the right to imagine themselves in one.</p>



<p>Bass ran when <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2020/08/14/us/charlotta-bass-kamala-harris-trnd">a Black woman entering the White House</a> seemed almost unimaginable. Almost. But not to her. I imagine she would have loved this election. And I suspect she would have had pointed questions for Gov.-elect Bottoms.</p>

<p>What will you do for the poor? The disenfranchised? How will you protect the vote that brought you here? </p>

<p>History-making is not the same as justice-making, and representation matters. The true measure of Bottoms’ victory will be whether Georgians experience the more just state <a href="https://www.wrdw.com/2026/11/03/billionaire-rick-jackson-atlanta-ex-mayor-keisha-lance-bottoms-vie-lead-georgia/">she promised to bring about</a>.</p>

<h2>The work beyond the win</h2>

<p>For generations, <a href="https://www.basicbooks.com/titles/martha-s-jones/vanguard/9781541618619/">Black women have been asked to save a democracy</a> that would not save them. We have carried clipboards, protest signs and entire movements on our backs. We have been told to wait. To be patient. To be grateful.</p>

<p>And now a Black woman has been elected to govern Georgia. </p>

<p>The children have not returned. The past has not been undone. But something has shifted. Charlotta dreamed it. Stacey helped build it. Keisha has won it. And somewhere, another little Black girl is watching. She may not understand the history. She may only know that the governor-elect looks like her. For now, that is enough to begin a dream.</p>

<p>And history has taught us what can happen when a Black girl begins to dream.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296027/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
