That would be Neptune, where one year is a little more than 60,000 days.

title: Dems won the midterms. How should they work with Trump?
excerpt: US Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-TX) speaks during a midterm election night event on November 3, 2026 in Austin, Texas. | Brandon Bell/Getty Images Just days aft
body: US Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-TX) speaks during a midterm election night event on November 3, 2026 in Austin, Texas. | Brandon Bell/Getty Images Just days after big wins in the midterms, Democrats are celebrating historic victories
But what can we actually learn from these wins?  David Axelrod is a Democratic strategist and the man behind Barack Obama’s two presidential victories
He’s not a senior political commentator at CNN
He’s spent decades figuring out how Democrats can win

On Wednesday, Axelrod joined America, Actually for a conversation with host Astead Herndon about what the blue wave in the midterms reveals about voters in the US right now, the powerful demographic shifts that are underway, and what Democrats need to do next to make good on the promises they made in their campaigns, all while Trump is still in the White House
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel
Is this all about Trump’s unpopularity, or an endorsement of Democrats? I heard Rahm Emanuel say that he doesn’t read this as a vindication of Democrats, but as a repudiation of Republicans
Does that distinction matter? And do we know if people were voting for Democrats or just against the administration? I think every midterm election in some ways is a referendum on the incumbent party
And it’s almost always the case that the verdict is: not as good as we’d like

You know, this election is the one where the people in power have to put on a button saying, “How am I doing?” And people get to tell them, and the answer was: really, really bad.  Horrible! Two thumbs down.  Really, really bad
And obviously it was a repudiation of the president
I think it was a real response to the same thing that drove the election as much as anything in 2024, which is costs and the fact that people are struggling in this economy
The thing that made this unusual was Trump was elected to lower these costs, and instead he made decisions that palpably raised them — the war, the tariffs
I think it’s given Democrats a chance to prove that they are who they say they are and work on these issues of cost
And they’re crippled in the sense that if they don’t have a partner in the president, all they can do is try and pass legislation and do things to reduce those costs, but they need a partner to do it
I don’t discount the fact that Trump may do a 180 on some things and be that partner
It is an open question who the president becomes after all of this, considering he’s, you know, the nicest way to say it is ideologically flexible
Should Democrats come in thinking accountability ? Should they come in thinking, find places of bipartisan alignment ? Is the answer both? Yeah, I think the answer is both
And it’s very tricky to strike that balance
And if the price of cooperation is to lay off of accountability, I don’t think that’s a deal they can make.  But I look at the way Mayor Mamdani has handled his relationship with Trump
And there may be some instructive elements to that, because he’s certainly critical of the president
But he’s also found areas around housing, for example, on which they can work together
Here’s what I would say to Democrats: Be willing to work with him
And I think you’ll pay a price if you don’t
If he’s willing to help you, for example, on rolling back some of these cuts to the affordable healthcare subsidies or to Medicaid cuts
I think the country would actually embrace that kind of deal
And for that reason, I think Trump may take it because I don’t think he gives a damn about the Republican Party
The Republican Party was just a vehicle for him, and now he’s mad at them — because he’s not going to blame himself for what happened on Tuesday
You talk about men, Latinos, Asian voters, young people , working-class people generally moving towards Democrats in numbers that were even larger than some polls expected
I was wondering: Did we write the obituary on the Obama coalition too early? Is it back? I’m so allergic to this because I remember when we won
I remember people talking about the coalition of the ascendant
This is the coalition that’s going to govern
Democrats took Hispanic voters, for example, for granted
Republicans took Hispanic voters for granted
And in each case they’re a constituency that is deeply responsive to economic circumstances
They’re getting hammered in this economy, as they were in 2024
They are also — in the main — socially conservative communities

I think both parties have been guilty sequentially in misreading this.  By the way, everybody’s talking about who’s responsible for the Republican performance this year? I don’t think Stephen Miller is getting the credit that he deserved
One hundred percent, yeah.  The immigration overreach is core to the collapse with Latino voters

title: Los Angeles is about to test a new kind of housing politics
excerpt: Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman at an election night party, November 3, 2026. | Sarah Reingewirtz/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images I
body: Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman at an election night party, November 3, 2026. | Sarah Reingewirtz/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images It’s notoriously hard to govern Los Angeles, a city that gives its mayor less direct authority over the government than in a city like New York or Chicago

But even so, it’d be hard to do much worse than Karen Bass.  Elected mayor of LA in 2022, Bass campaigned on promises to solve the city’s homelessness and housing affordability crises (which are really part of the same underlying crisis )
She then spent her term undermining her own administration’s affordable housing policy and fighting the state of California’s efforts to compel cities to allow more housing production

She lost her bid for reelection this week to Nithya Raman, an LA City Council member, rising progressive star, and nationally prominent YIMBY.  Los Angeles has the highest ratio of home price to household income of any large city in America, and the second fewest homes per adult of any major city

It has a highly suburbanized and car-oriented fabric, like much of the rest of the country — all of which makes it a kind of proving ground for whether America’s sprawling cities can build their way out of their housing shortages.  Everyone in the city’s political leadership notionally agrees that LA needs to permit a lot more homes to meet demand — the only true way to make housing affordable — but not all of them have evidently had the policy discipline to follow through.  Raman may be different

She has gained a following in housing reform circles over the last few years with her brisk, direct-to-camera social videos explaining how LA’s housing shortage drives up rents and criticizing city policies that make it so difficult to build more homes (perhaps it’s no surprise that she has plenty of friends in Hollywood ). “There has been an overall lack of urgency in addressing housing supply in [Bass’s] administration,” Raman told me in an interview in July

How best to accommodate LA’s need for more housing, she said, is “a question that the city has actually turned away from.” Even given LA’s relatively weak mayoralty, Bass’s failures on housing were often a matter of political choice

As The Atlantic’s Marc Novicoff put it , “Bass seems to have gone out of her way to exercise as little power as possible.” Where she did go out of her way to wield her influence, it was often to stop denser housing from being built

Some of her bewildering housing policy choices while in office include:  Days into her term, Bass signed her first executive order, known as ED1, to fast-track housing developments where 100 percent of the apartments are affordable
Applications for these projects were to get approvals within 60 days instead of being dragged through excruciating permitting processes
It was a good idea — and it seemed to be working, quickly attracting developer applications to build thousands of affordable apartments
It was working so well, in fact, that a backlash from vocal NIMBYs followed

Less than six months after signing ED1, in June 2023, Bass weakened it to exclude projects in single-family neighborhoods — which make up three-quarters of LA’s residential land — from the fast-track approval process

Her administration even tried to apply that restriction retroactively to developments that had already applied to build in single-family areas under ED1, a breathtaking display of bureaucratic dysfunction; a judge later ruled that this violated California law
Bass has since added more restrictions to the ED1, and one observer has described it as “functionally gutted” for many developers

To be fair to Bass, even after she weakened it, the program has still resulted in more than 7,700 affordable apartments under construction, according to her campaign.   Bass opposed SB 79, a landmark California law that passed in 2025 requiring cities and suburbs to allow construction of denser housing near transit stops
Permitting apartments near public transit is one of the most basic principles of sensible urban planning
But in LA, it was controversial enough that Bass urged Gov

After he signed SB 79 into law anyway, Bass worked with LA’s city council to delay much of the law’s most ambitious upzoning until 2030, while permitting smaller apartment buildings near some transit stops

After the devastating January 2025 fires, some property owners whose homes had burned down in the Pacific Palisades had applied to rebuild under SB 9, another important California law that allows single-family lots to be modestly densified into up to four housing units

In response to backlash from some neighbors , Bass reportedly pressed Newsom to restrict SB 9 in fire-damaged areas; she then banned SB 9 applications in parts of the Palisades. (There are certainly legitimate questions about whether rebuilding in such a fire-prone area is a good idea at all

But Bass offered no publicly available analysis that the modest increase in density allowed by SB 9 posed a special danger, even as she worked to accelerate the rebuilding of single-family homes.)  All of these point to a leader who is not serious about changing the conditions that led to LA’s housing shortage, and lacks the courage to take on what is arguably the city’s most defining political challenge
Raman has promised to fundamentally break from that approach
That will make her mayoralty an important experiment for the rest of the country
Even modest progress in a city as resistant to housing as LA could help crack open a way forward for new approaches to housing in the many other cities that face affordability crises
This won’t be easy for her — she’ll face the same anti-building political pressures, and will need to maintain a cooperative relationship with the city council
When I spoke to Raman over the summer, I noticed that she treaded gingerly around the topic of adding density to single-family neighborhoods
Because of the uniquely American obsession with keeping single-family homes segregated from other types of development, it can be a real political third rail in LA and nationwide
But research has suggested the city can’t fill its housing shortage without building more in those neighborhoods

Raman will, at least, have an important ally in California’s newly elected governor, Xavier Becerra, who is also a strong YIMBY.  Raman’s affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) makes her emblematic of a fusion that’s been emerging in Democratic politics, between supply-side abundance and left-wing economic populism
It’s also evident in politicians like Zohran Mamdani and some of the young Democrats who won elections across the country this week.  I think this is right
It's not just that Talarico (et al) combines elements of left populism, abundance pragmatism, and cultural moderation
It's also that the definitions of "left" and "moderate" are in flux

Take "left." Talarico's all-of-the-above position on energy, eg,… https://t.co/elbUP9vT11 — Derek Thompson (@DKThomp) November 5, 2026 From talking to Raman, I have the sense that she’s more at home with the YIMBY part of her politics than the DSA part
Her relationship with the DSA’s LA chapter has been strained (though it did endorse her candidacy)

But her social-democratic commitments are also sincere — she’s been a strong champion of rent control and tenant protections in LA, for example, and helped shape a stronger rent stabilization law the city adopted last year.  The new political syntheses taking shape on the American left are exciting and intriguing
Whether it will finally make a breakthrough in LA’s — and California’s, and America’s — housing crisis, of course, remains to be tested
But it’s a welcome sign that American politics need not remain trapped in the same orthodoxies and failures.

title: Maybe Americans don’t like cruelty after all
excerpt: As various factions try to make the case about what won the midterms — moderation or progressivism, populism or the establishment — perhaps the easiest and most
body: As various factions try to make the case about what won the midterms — moderation or progressivism, populism or the establishment — perhaps the easiest and most universal way to describe 2026 was as a contest between decency and cruelty
For nearly a decade, bullying, scape-goating, and just plain meanness have been the dominant tone of Republican politics

From Donald Trump relentlessly picking on minority groups in the 2016 campaign, through family separations in 2018 — all while demeaning political rivals and journalists and anyone who criticized him — a generation of Republican politicians have seen the president reach new levels of nastiness in politics and be rewarded for it

Other candidates picked up on it, often attempting their own imitations: Vice President JD Vance mocked “childless cat ladies” in 2021 , while other Republicans joked about political violence against Democrats or critics , their physical appearances , or their ethnicities
And yet somehow, in the 2026 midterm campaigns, the MAGA right went even harder on cruelty up and down the ballot
Pivotal campaign moments, particularly in the closing weeks of the cycle, weren’t just about bare-knuckle politics and nasty campaigning, but actually punching down at the weak and vulnerable
Republican Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy trotted out his opponent’s estranged mother to suggest the candidate was lying about childhood abuse
Tim Scott used a transphobic slur to to mock a candidate while campaigning for Darline Graham
Michigan GOP senatorial candidate Mike Rogers fanned the flames of Islamophobia, accusing his opponent of “ pledging ” his support to Islamist extremism, something other Republicans echoed

And in Texas, a statewide candidate doubled down on racist anti-Indian-American tweets .  In 2018, the writer Adam Serwer coined the phrase, and concept, that “ the cruelty is the point ” — that the easiest way to understand the MAGA movement was as a desire to inflict pain and suffering on marginalized people, specific minorities, and political opponents through political power
Cruelty wasn’t incidental; it was intentional.  For Republican candidates and campaigners this cycle, cruelty became almost a central campaign tactic

Many of them struggled to mount a serious policy case, and found themselves stuck with a historically unpopular president as party leader, so they fell back on the tried-and-true maneuver of beating up on the weak, hoping it would work as well as it seemed to throughout the Trump era
Yet on Tuesday night, voters delivered a verdict: They were fed up with that cruelty in both the administration and Republican campaigns
Instead, decency — or, at least, voters’ impression of it — won
Even some conservatives, as they try to sort through the wreckage and blame game post-Election Day, made that case
The Christian broadcaster Erick Erickson noted that in addition to the Iran war and affordability crisis, Republicans lost because of “the impression of cruelty
The accidental arrests of American citizens who were Hispanic

The arrogance.” And, of course, many Democrats agreed, too.  “The American people were loud and clear [Tuesday] night that they want to like their neighbor, that their neighbor is not the enemy from within, and even if they disagree politically with their neighbor, they want them to do well and they want their kids to do very well,” Kentucky Gov

Andy Beshear, who led the party’s efforts to elect Democratic governors around the country, told me. “People [Tuesday] night showed us that they want decency in the White House and they want decency in Congress.” All the Republicans above lost their races
The set of people who won — and especially those who flipped seats from red to blue – noticeably embraced a more compassionate tone of politics
Republicans centered cruelty; Democratic candidates chose decency and won It’s hard to summarize just how nasty the 2026 GOP campaign strategy was
Hate, racism, and xenophobia were the go-to tools used on the right this cycle — on top of a year of hardline immigration policies and spending cuts pushed by the Trump administration

And it all came up short, Joe Walsh, the former GOP member of Congress and current anti-Trump activist, told me. “Republicans tried to win again this year by being as cruel and fearful and divisive as they could
That’s generally worked in the past, but there were extenuating circumstances this year,” Walsh said. “People [on the trail] would tell me, ‘This is not the kind of country we are

This is not who we are.’” They were referring, he said, to masked ICE agents, the targeting of Black and brown people, and talk of white Christian nationalism.  “There was something more profound at stake here,” Walsh continued. “And I think it was the American people recoiling against the cruelty they’ve seen.” It was all a sharp contrast to the way Democrats talked and the policies they supported on the trail
Take Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico’s words in his Tuesday night victory speech: We didn’t win by alienating our neighbors, or by shaming our neighbors, or by ridiculing our neighbors
A politics rooted in a deep love — for our state, for our country, and for all of our neighbors
My faith teaches me that love is the strongest force in the universe…love requires that we stand between the bullies and the bullied
Love requires that we look evil in the eye and not blink
Beshear told me that beyond concerns about gas prices, the Iran war, and tariffs, voters’ frustrations reflected a rejection of the fear and divisiveness that Trump embodies

He said he saw this rejection of cruelty while stumping for candidates in red states, and he saw the opposite coming from the Democratic candidates who won. “Everywhere I traveled, our gubernatorial candidates were talking about being a good neighbor,” he said. “[Iowa Gov.-elect] Rob Sand talked about it at every one of his town halls, and you could see people nodding about it. [Ohio Gov.-elect] Amy Acton talked about it in each of her speeches
People are craving decency, especially given the cruelty that this president governs with.” This contrast was apparent in some data and focus group research, too

In polling conducted by The Argument before the election, Democrats had a 20-point advantage when voters were asked which party they thought was more “compassionate,” a 12-point lead when they were asked which party “cared” for voters, and a 10-point lead when they were asked which party was more moderate
View Link “The party of compassion won,” the writer Jerusalem Demsas wrote for The Argument

Republicans just couldn’t shake the association, their polling showed, with “words like ‘bold,’ “strong,’ and ‘extreme.’” And in Ohio, perhaps the most obvious example of cruelty becoming the closing message of a Republican campaign, focus groups conducted by the political strategist Sarah Longwell for The Bulwark before the election showed how quickly the infamous ad became associated with the Republican brand
Longwell wrote about the session: The first thing to note is that everyone in the group had heard about Ramaswamy’s ad already
The second thing to note is that several of the Ramaswamy-curious voters in the group said it was pushing them toward either supporting a third-party candidate or sitting out the election altogether

The fact that everyone had heard of or seen the ad and the universal revulsion to it suggest that this could be an all-time backfire for Ramaswamy — and it raises the possibility that Trump and Vance will also suffer politically for rushing to defend it
In follow-up focus group conversations on Wednesday, the day after the election, voters told Longwell they wanted a hard break from this era of politics

This rejection of cruelty was also most evident in backlash to the Trump administration’s immigration policies — in places that saw ICE raids or which saw stricter enforcement in heavily Hispanic areas of Florida, Kansas, and Texas, voters swung hard against the GOP. “These are voters who were very supportive of securing the border, very supportive of Border Patrol, which is a huge employer down there,” the Democratic strategist Lis Smith told me. “But the cruelty of what ICE was doing, tearing apart families and communities was just a bridge too far

title: Convenience is a hot commodity. Here’s how to decide when it’s actually worth it.
excerpt: Despite the widespread protests over data centers and Flock cameras , the viral videos of people pranking bots in job interviews , frustration with slop, and ra
body: Despite the widespread protests over data centers and Flock cameras , the viral videos of people pranking bots in job interviews , frustration with slop, and rage at tech CEOs’ rightward lean , AI is spreading.  According to the Pew Research Center , about half of American adults have used a chatbot, and around a quarter do so daily
By multiple measurements, the public has adopted AI faster than they did home computers or the internet
I’m seeing it more and more in my personal life: On video calls, I notice the Claude app in the menu bar of shared screens
An ad on Instagram pushing me to use Meta’s AI assistant revealed which of my friends had already begun doing so (something that might not even be true )
Still, many of the people who are using AI have mixed feelings about it

Pew notes that of the chatbot adopters they surveyed, 40 percent believe AI will have a more negative than positive effect on society; a 2026 Gallup poll of more than 1,500 14‑ to 29‑year‑olds came to a similar conclusion
No one I talk to about their personal AI use seems to particularly like it, but they accept it
In some cases, it’s the least-bad option; asking a chatbot a question is easier than searching, especially as search engines become so enshittified they’re unusable
In other cases, the tech just seems inevitable
Articles, analysts, and executives insist this is the future
New technology moves from novelty to necessity in very little time, and adoption continues even though the future this tech promised isn’t as utopian as the marketing made it seem

Eighteen years ago, only early adopters had smartphones; then suddenly everyone had one, and we were all using them to stream, to stay in touch, and to alleviate boredom at every turn.  Plenty of people seem to regret this adoption
You see it in efforts to limit screen time and in the regular waves of nostalgia for physical media
It’s even in the first few paragraphs of this article — as terms like “slop,” “enshittification,” and “brainrot” enter common parlance

We’ve coined and redefined words to describe a future we didn’t imagine and don’t seem to want.  But while we may now have shorthand to describe the problem, solving it takes something more; nostalgia and anger can only go so far
The devices, apps, and tools that are easy to adopt are hard to give up, especially as the world is increasingly oriented around them
In just a few years, the smartphone became a replacement for everything from cash to car keys

Many workplaces assume their employees will be able to read email anywhere and that they will install productivity apps on their personal device (I have a folder with Airtable, Asana, Slack, Teams, Zoom, and other apps I wish I could delete)
And new accessories and subscriptions come along constantly to wring functionality and durability out of our phones — wireless headphones, cases, extra batteries, cloud storage
As much as we may dream of living without a smartphone , the most that many of us can do is delete some apps or use a Brick (yet another accessory) to limit our use

Look around your neighborhood, and you’ll see how this pattern has played out with other conveniences: streets full of Amazon vans, DoorDash bikes, and Ubers; doorbell cameras to track the theft of those deliveries; abandoned electric scooters on sidewalks; cities built for private cars more than for people.  It’s easy to imagine AI following a similar path — fulfilling some simple desires for convenience at first, then overtaking the alternatives, and fitting into our lives in ways we can’t yet imagine and might not want, but accept because it just seems like this is the natural path of technology.  There are, of course, advantages to new technology, but these wane over time as the downsides become clearer

On the personal side, there’s the frustration of stalled advancement: Each new phone upgrade seems to do less while requiring a costly purchase; ride-hailing services, streaming, and delivery costs climb, and the services don’t get better or more reliable; data breaches are a near-daily headline; and scam attempts fill our email apps, DMs, and any other inbox we have

It’s hard to avoid seeing the public consequences of this convenience, too: the exploitation of workers and the planet required to mine the minerals for batteries and other components, then the labor it takes to put those components into new devices; the allegations of wage theft , algorithmic discrimination , and workdays so grueling drivers have to urinate in bottles ; the K-shaped economy that gig work is built on and perpetuates
This makes it all the more essential to approach any offer of improved convenience with skepticism, and with a doubtfulness learned by unfulfilled promises and bad design

No technology is truly inevitable, no matter how much pressure we may feel to adopt it from our peers and from the corporate buzz that insists this is the future.  How to identify false conveniences So how do we avoid welcoming these false conveniences into our lives? It starts with recognizing them for what they are

In 1987, Wendell Berry caused a minor kerfuffle in the pages of Harper’s magazine with his essay, “ Why I Am Not Going to Buy a Computer .” In the short piece, Berry explained his reasoning behind the title
The computer could do his work faster, but speed wasn’t his concern
He also knew a computer would be expensive and isolating (Berry’s wife worked with him typing manuscripts)
He ends the essay with a list of criteria for adopting a new tool, among them that a new tool should be less expensive than what it replaces, and it should be repairable and available at a local shop
He closes his list by writing that a new tool “should not replace or disrupt anything good that already exists.” This last one is tough

How do we decide what’s good and not worth disrupting? And on the other side, how do we decide whether the device or convenience that disrupts something we want disrupted — chores, for instance — is worth it?  Here, another list can help

In his 10 principles of good design , the legendary industrial designer Dieter Rams wrote that good design is honest about what it does, and is environmentally friendly, long-lasting, and makes a product useful
The utility of many new devices, tools, and apps may be clear, but often the design is dishonest

It hides the real costs of the convenience, like the environmental waste and lost dollars that come with replacing our phones every couple of years, or the privacy sacrifices inherent in many digital services

Or the design obscures the ways the tech might disrupt something good, like the way social media seemed to connect us with our friends, but now exposes us to scammers and to strangers who post rage bait and gets in the way of staying in touch with the people we actually care about.  As I was writing my book, Against Convenience , I kept turning to these two lists

How should I assess a promised convenience and avoid the early adaptation that leads to reliance on a technology I don’t really like? I came up with my own list for the book: questions that could keep me from being too eager for new tech, and less prone to fall into a cycle of increasingly worse design

It’s more than just saying no or resisting tech to preserve some nostalgic ideal — it’s a way to question what we really get from a new device or app, and what that tech might grow into if the pattern continues.   What does this save me? Does this convenience save me time, money, or effort? If it’s time, what will I use that time for? If it’s money, why has the price dropped? If it’s effort, who is doing the work instead? What does this cost me? What do I have to give up for this convenience? Will I have to pay in perpetuity? What does this replace? What is the old process for doing the same task? Is there anything I like about that task? Will I lose something I enjoy? How will I replace that enjoyment? What problem does this solve? What is the cause of the problem in the first place? Will this solve the problem entirely? Will I be able to stop using this convenience if I don’t like it? How long will I wait to decide?  Who is making this possible? Do I trust them? Is anyone’s work eliminated in this process, besides my own? Have any workers who make this convenience possible made statements about their working conditions? What is the environmental toll? Is this necessary? Is this getting rid of something that’s difficult, expensive, or time-­consuming? Is there some other way to achieve these savings without this particular convenience? The list is inconvenient by design
It pushes me to slow down, to consider costs before they’re sunk
And to ask if this is really the direction I want to go in

The worst that can happen is life goes on as usual, while a few of my friends have something new to complain about.  I built this list around my experiences of stepping on the rake of tech that overpromises and underdelivers, around many instances of believing hype and holding onto a device in the hope that it will one day work like it’s supposed to

title: A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure
excerpt: A sweeping new Senate bill aims to speed up the notoriously slow US energy permitting process—but whether it helps or hurts emissions depends entirely on what g
body: A sweeping new Senate bill aims to speed up the notoriously slow US energy permitting process—but whether it helps or hurts emissions depends entirely on what gets built
The bill's backers span the political spectrum, from the White House to clean energy groups, who argue renewables stand to win economically if more building is unlocked

Critics warn the bill could open the floodgates for fossil fuel expansion, with one modeler finding it may have actually increased energy sector emissions and air pollution risks had it been in place in 2025. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148062" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US
With the dust barely settled on this week’s momentous midterms, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on November 9
It’s a plan that could finally start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved, as part of something called permitting reform
People on both sides of the political aisle have been pushing for this type of change for some years

The key question is whether this will cut greenhouse-gas emissions from the US energy sector or push them higher still.   The federal permitting system is designed to protect the environment against industrial pollution from large projects like power plants, transmission lines, and natural-gas pipelines
Today, permitting is governed by a range of laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act
And if there’s one thing you might know about the current state of permitting in the US it’s that it’s slow and incredibly complicated
So in its 417 pages, BAAJA attempts to tighten things up

The bill has provisions that narrow the sorts of projects that need to apply for federal permits and others that enact deadlines in hopes of speeding up a process that today can take years. (There are also specific provisions about transmission planning, mining, and the rest of the kitchen sink; this thing is dense .) One thing to know about this bill is that it’s largely technology neutral: It opens the doors for the buildout of projects involving both fossil fuels and renewables
So there’s a weird mishmash of legislators and outside groups supporting it
The bill’s four sponsors in the Senate are two Republicans and two Democrats
The White House has backed this permitting reform bill, with its Council of Economic Advisors finding that it would reduce review times and have economic benefits like boosting GDP

Clean energy groups like the American Clean Power Association have largely come out in favor of the bill too, with the group’s analysis finding that it could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean energy for the grid
Some environmental groups, however, oppose the bill, or parts of it

An assessment from the Natural Resources Defense Council says the parts about transmission could have substantial benefits for the grid, but the narrowing of environmental reviews could be damaging for public and private lands
Many in the climate world have long been calling for permitting reform, arguing that renewables stand to benefit more than fossil fuels
The thinking is that solar and wind power are some of the cheapest sources available today, so if we unlock the ability to build more energy, they are likely to win out economically
A few early analyses have tried to quantify just what BAAJA would mean for emissions in the US

One, from the think tank Rhodium Group, found that in the best-case scenario, the bill would cut economy-wide emissions by 4%, reduce annual energy bills by $78 per household, and add 200 gigawatts of new clean energy by 2040
In the worst case, emissions would stay about the same

Another report , from the nonprofit research group Resources for the Future, found that the bill could cut power-sector emissions 6% by 2041 and save more than $350 billion on system costs by midcentury
But there are some concerns that this permitting bill’s real effect would be to open the floodgates for new natural-gas plants

As data centers have put more pressure on the grid, a wave of such plants have been announced. “You get down to a trade-off between essentially growing the clean electricity industry on the one hand and then, as a compromise, growing the fossil-fuel industry on the other,” says Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue

To quantify that trade-off, Kircher also modeled the potential emissions effects of the bill and found that if BAAJA had been in place in 2025, energy sector emissions would have been higher than the actual baseline
Health and mortality risks associated with air pollution would also have increased
This bill is scheduled for a Senate vote on November 9, well before the next Congress takes control
It’s not clear what the dramatic victories for Democrats might mean for the legislation, which was expected to pass the Senate with largely Republican support if a few Democrats got on board
Democrats could decide to wait for next year, when they’ll have control of both chambers

But any deal would ultimately need to win Trump’s signature, limiting what a future bill might be able to change.  In a world where permitting new projects is easier, we’ll see more clean energy, but we’ll see more natural gas, too
And while prices could get lower, that could push demand for electricity higher, leading to more emissions overall
Simplifying the permitting system and cutting red tape is a worthy goal
But when it comes to emissions, it still really matters what, exactly, you want to build.

title: Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
excerpt: Texas's data center boom may be over: Texas has been the fastest-growing data center market in the US, but a Democratic sweep of the governor's mansio
body: Texas's data center boom may be over: Texas has been the fastest-growing data center market in the US, but a Democratic sweep of the governor's mansion and Senate seat—with candidates who campaigned hard against data centers—has the industry bracing for moratoriums and permit freezes

The projects at stake are enormous: Two facilities alone—Stargate Frontier and Nexus Hubbard—represent thousands of megawatts of planned AI infrastructure, making any slowdown a serious blow to Big Tech's ambitions and the broader economy

Voters sent a clear message: Across the US, midterm voters backed efforts to shield ratepayers from data center-driven electricity costs and supported outright bans on new facilities—a sign that Big Tech has badly failed to convince the public that AI will actually improve their lives

Governing is harder than campaigning: Local officials, complicated county-by-county politics, and construction unions that backed Democratic candidates could all complicate any push for a sweeping moratorium. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148043" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts
But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position
Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton
Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott
At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years
Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail
Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing
At the industry’s DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September

That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities , began changing course himself.  Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails
On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits
Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether.  The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that
Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium
That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state
The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive

The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas

Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana.  The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall
Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back
And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects
Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices
Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether

If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it

A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere.  It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas
Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton
Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift

But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red.  This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted

Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices.  Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state
And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns

So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.

body: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991
But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare)
